text:
A: Hello there. Is that, er, is that working? Can you see me?
B: Yes, I can see you. Hiya. Sorry, I've got the sound up now.
A: Lovely. I'm Colin. I'm in Worthing, down on the south coast.
B: Lorraine. I'm near Wrexham. Rhos, Rhosllannerchrugog, but nobody can say it, so I just say Wrexham.
A: Rhos... no, I'm not even going to try, I'll embarrass myself. Wrexham I know, though. That's the football lot, isn't it, with the film stars.
B: That's it. You can't move in town on a match day now. It's lovely for them, mind.
A: I bet. Did you get on alright with the puzzle at the start?
B: Erm, sort of. I do word searches, so I thought I'd be alright, but it wasn't really like that, was it.
A: No. I did about half and then my brain went for a walk. My wife does the crossword with me and she normally carries me, so on my own I was a bit lost.
B: Oh dear.
A: So what do you do with yourself, Lorraine? Are you working?
B: Not at the minute. I was at the college in Wrexham. I ran the morning cleaning team there for a good few years. Then the contract changed hands and they offered voluntary redundancy, so I took it. I'm looking for something part-time now, a school kitchen maybe, or a care home. Just daytimes. Sorry, I'm waffling.
A: You're not waffling at all. Running a team at half five in the morning, that's no joke.
B: Half five, yes. You get used to it. It's getting un-used to it that's funny.
A: I know just what you mean. I was a joiner, forty-odd years, and when I packed it in I kept waking at six thinking I'd got a kitchen to fit. Took me a year to stop.
B: Did it? That's good to know, actually.
A: Oh yes. Now I just potter. I've got a shed, do a bit of woodturning, bowls and that. I've got one on the go out of a bit of old cherry. It's come out a bit lopsided, but I'm telling everyone it's deliberate.
B: I saw a little bowl on your shelf, in the picture. Was that one of yours?
A: That was, yes. One of the better ones. The bad ones go to the family. No, that's not true. Well, it's a bit true.
B: My grandson would love one. He's into dinosaurs at the minute, everything's dinosaurs. He'd want a T-rex on it.
A: How old is he?
B: Five. He's in Mold with my daughter. I have him most weekends.
A: Oh, that's lovely. We've got two in Brighton, we pick them up from school on a Wednesday. Ours were dinosaurs, then it was space, now it's some cartoon I can't keep up with.
B: That's what's coming, then.
A: That's what's coming. Do you get out much yourself, walking or anything?
B: Every day if I can. Up round the lanes, or along Ponciau Banks. My knee doesn't like the hill, but I go anyway.
A: Good for you. I'm on the Downs most days. Got absolutely soaked up there last week, came home like a drowned rat and Maureen wouldn't let me in the kitchen. Anyway, where was I. Oh, walking. My dad didn't make sixty, so I sort of think, keep moving, you know.
B: Oh, I'm sorry. My mam went three years ago. You do think about it, don't you.
A: You do. Sorry to hear that, love.
B: Thank you. I don't know if that's what... anyway. What are you having for tea tonight?
A: For dinner? Oh, I've no idea, Maureen's in charge. Probably something sensible. I did a paella once and we've not —
